summary:
Trans visitors to Kentucky stand under the United States federal framework on travel documents and screening. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and bars self-selection of gender on passports and visas; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents. Visa discretion, including the February 2025 refusal pathway for trans athletes seeking entry for women's sporting events, and checkpoint screening procedures apply on arrival in Louisville, Lexington and elsewhere in Kentucky as they do in every other state.

Kentucky's own instrument is Senate Bill 150, enacted on 29 March 2023 when the Kentucky General Assembly voted to override Governor Andy Beshear's veto. The statute does two things relevant here: it restricts which bathrooms transgender students may use in public schools, and it bans gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors in the commonwealth. It is the single 2023 statute carrying the school facility restriction.

Implementation runs through local school districts. In April 2023 the Kentucky Department of Education issued guidance to districts on applying the 2023 rules, advising them to remove sex education from the fifth-grade curriculum and to tread cautiously with the bathroom provisions. The department does not enforce the restriction directly; districts do.

The care prohibition took effect on 14 July 2023, when United States District Judge David Hale lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month. The order allows Kentucky to bar transgender minors from puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Seven transgender children and their parents had sued to block the statute, and the ACLU of Kentucky called the ruling a temporary setback.

The Movement Advancement Project's equality map catalogues Kentucky's 2023 K-12 facility ban among its state-by-state entries on bans against transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, placing the commonwealth within a national pattern rather than an isolated rule.
tangentialFactors:
Kentucky's school facility ban belongs to a wider national tally. The Movement Advancement Project counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings across nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in particular circumstances. Kentucky sits on the restricted side of that count.

Enforcement elsewhere has escalated to arrest. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law. Nothing comparable is documented in Kentucky, but the Florida case establishes the direction of travel for school and government-building provisions of this kind.

Facility and document rules are tightening in several states. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, while also barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups describe it as a template, with further bills pending. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged.

Kentucky's ban on gender-affirming care for minors is part of a much larger block: such care is prohibited in 27 states, and several of the corresponding federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
localsOnly:
Senate Bill 150 governs Kentucky residents directly. Its care prohibition prevents transgender minors in the commonwealth from accessing puberty blockers and hormone therapy, and it took effect statewide on 14 July 2023 after the federal injunction was lifted.

School districts carry out the facility restriction, working from the Kentucky Department of Education's April 2023 guidance. That guidance also directs districts to remove sex education from the fifth-grade curriculum and to proceed carefully with the bathroom provisions, leaving day-to-day operation with local boards rather than the state education department.

Litigation over the statute was brought by seven transgender children and their parents, represented with the ACLU of Kentucky, which characterised Judge David Hale's July 2023 ruling as a temporary setback. Whether that litigation or any subsequent challenge remains live is not established by the sources available here.

For adults, the sources do not describe Kentucky restrictions on restroom or facility use outside the school setting, and they say nothing about state rules for changing the sex marker on a Kentucky driver's licence or birth certificate.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Kentucky has enacted or is advancing any restriction on updating sex markers on state driver's licences or birth certificates is not sourced here, and no Kansas-style invalidation of existing Kentucky documents is documented in this inventory.

Unresolved: the sources do not record any arrest, citation or disciplinary action under Senate Bill 150's bathroom provisions in Kentucky, and they do not establish whether the Florida arrest pattern has any Kentucky analogue.

Unresolved: the scope of Kentucky's facility restriction beyond public schools, including application to state government buildings, adult visitors, or privately operated venues, is not addressed by the available sources.

Not sourced: Kentucky hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, the state's treatment of out-of-state identification documents at stops or checks, and any Kentucky-specific litigation challenging Senate Bill 150 after July 2023. The status of that litigation, including whether the injunction litigation concluded or continued, remains an open question against these materials.
